common_name: Pink Fragrance Daphne (Rose-Pink Everblooming Hybrid Daphne)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or early fall in humus-rich, neutral to slightly alkaline, well-drained soil in partial shade; a rose-pink-flowered sibling of 'Eternal Fragrance' and 'Summer Ice' in the same repeat-blooming hybrid group raised by English breeder Robin White.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil with neutral to slightly alkaline pH in partial shade, allowing morning sun for best bloom while shielding from hot afternoon exposure. Pink Fragrance carries deeper rose-pink flowers than the pale 'Eternal Fragrance', opening in a heavy spring flush on compact, semi-evergreen mounds and then reblooming intermittently through summer into fall. Its small stature suits foundation plantings, mixed borders, and containers placed near paths or seating where the fragrance can be enjoyed up close. Keep the root zone cool and evenly moist without waterlogging, avoid transplanting once established, and note that all parts are toxic if ingested.

common_name: Garden House Pink Daphne (Devon-Bred Nepalese Paper Daphne)

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in fall or spring in sheltered, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; this cultivar was raised by Keith Wiley at The Garden House in Devon, England, and carries clear pink, strongly scented flowers.

directions: Site in a wind-sheltered partial-shade border with humus-rich, moist but free-draining soil, since harsh winter wind can damage its largely evergreen foliage. From midwinter into early spring, Garden House Pink opens dense clusters of clear pink flowers carrying the powerful, far-reaching fragrance typical of D. bholua, strong enough to perfume a path or entry from several feet away. It grows into a tall, upright, multi-stemmed shrub over time, so give it room to develop rather than crowding it among smaller shade plants. Avoid root disturbance once established, and handle with care since all parts are toxic if ingested.

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in fall or early spring in gritty, sharply drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in partial shade; this slow-growing dwarf daphne resents root disturbance, so site it permanently in a raised bed or rock garden.

directions: Plant in gritty, sharply drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in partial shade, ideally in a raised bed, trough, or rock garden where the crown stays dry. Cheriton forms a dense, slow-growing dome under a foot tall, smothered each spring in small, intensely fragrant, rosy-pink flowers held tight against the evergreen foliage. Holder of an RHS Award of Garden Merit, it is prized by alpine and rock-garden specialists for its compact, long-lived habit and reliable bloom. Avoid heavy, wet soils and any disturbance to the root zone; all parts are toxic if ingested.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or early spring in humus-rich, moist but well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in partial shade; this long-cultivated white-flowered form of mezereon resents root disturbance once sited.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, moist but well-drained soil in partial shade and leave undisturbed once sited, since daphnes resent transplanting. This clean white-flowered form of February daphne opens fragrant blooms along bare stems in late winter just as the typical purple-pink form does, but is followed by translucent yellow berries instead of red, giving a distinctive two-season color break from the species. It performs best where summers stay relatively cool and humidity moderate, and can struggle in prolonged heat. All parts, especially the berries and sap, are toxic if ingested and the sap can irritate skin, so site away from children and pets and wear gloves when pruning.

common_name: Alba Winter Daphne (Pure White-Flowered Fragrant Daphne)

planting.note: Plant in early fall or spring in sharply drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; daphne resents transplanting, so choose the permanent site carefully.

directions: Plant in sharply drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade and choose the site carefully, since winter daphne resents transplanting once established. Alba is a pure white-flowered form of winter daphne, lacking the rosy-purple flush that colors the outside of typical D. odora blooms, and carries the same intensely sweet, far-carrying fragrance from late winter into early spring. Its clean white flower clusters pair well in all-white or moon-garden shade plantings where the usual pink-purple winter daphne would clash. Excellent drainage is essential; keep evenly watered through summer dry spells and avoid heavy, wet soil, which causes rapid root rot. All parts are toxic if ingested.

planting.note: Plant in a raised bed or rock garden with sharp drainage and mulch with gravel rather than organic matter to keep the crown dry; the gold-edged foliage of Variegata holds color best with some direct sun.

directions: Variegata is a gold-edged sport of rose daphne, its narrow evergreen leaves rimmed in creamy yellow, giving the low, trailing mat year-round interest well beyond the fragrant rose-pink flower clusters that smother it each late spring. Like the species, it is a classic rock garden and raised-bed plant, draping attractively over stone edges where both foliage and bloom show to advantage. Sharp drainage is essential since more plants are lost to wet, heavy soil than to cold; mulch with gravel rather than organic material to keep the crown dry. Avoid moving it once established, and note that all parts are toxic if ingested.
